August 29, 2026



```
[princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp](https://princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp)
## This session

### 1) Types, vectors, and objects ::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"} * Everything is a type - But we can get [extremely pedantic](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/base-types.html) * Vectors, matrices, lists, and more * Subsetting syntax; common functions :::
### 2) Data frames, reading data, and R as a calculator ::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"} * Data frames: what and how * Getting data in and out of R * Summary statistics and some real data ::: ## Some sources

* Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund, *R for Data Science*, 2e * [Ch. 27: A field guide to base R](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/base-R.html) * [Ch. 12: Logical vectors](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/logicals.html) * [Ch. 7: Data import](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-import.html) * Harvard IQSS, *Math Prefresher for Political Scientists* * [Ch. 7.5: Reading in and inspecting data](https://iqss.github.io/prefresher/11_data-handling_counting.html) * [Ch. 8: Manipulating vectors and matrices](https://iqss.github.io/prefresher/12_matricies-manipulation.html) # Types ## Every object has a type

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 1 class(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} school <- "Princeton" class(school) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} The type is R's label for what kind of thing a value is — every object carries one ::: ::: {.fragment} Types decide what's possible: numbers can be averaged, text can be capitalized, etc. ::: :::{.fragment} Most confusing errors are type errors in disguise. ::: ## Some basic types

| Type | Examples | | |:---|:---|:---| | `numeric` | `1`, `3.14`, `-2.5` | numbers (a.k.a. "double") | | `integer` | `1L`, `42L` | whole numbers; the `L` makes it explicit | | `character` | `"Princeton"` | text, in quotes — `'single'` work too | | `logical` | `TRUE`, `FALSE` | yes/no answers (`T`/`F` also acceptable) | | `Date` | `Sys.Date()` | calendar dates | : {tbl-colwidths="[14,24,62]"}
::: {.fragment} Coming soon: `list`, `data.frame` ::: ::: {.fragment} Mostly you'll just say "numeric" — R treats `1` as a double by default ::: ::: {.fragment} Why keep both? Storage: `double` is 8 bytes (for the decimals); `integer` is 4 bytes. ::: ::: {.fragment} Mostly you'll just notice it as `int` vs `num` in output ::: ## Reassignment

An object name holds a value. Assigning again replaces it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- x + 2 x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Types decide what's allowed: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} school + "University" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `school + "University"`: ! non-numeric argument to binary operator ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} R will not guess what you meant. ::: ## Casting: convert types deliberately

The `as.*()` family converts between types ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.numeric("3") as.character(3.9) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 [1] "3.9" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Careful casting *to* integer — decimals get chopped, not rounded: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.integer(3.9) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.numeric("Princeton") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: NAs introduced by coercion ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.blocktext} When R *can't* convert, you get `NA` and a warning (not an error!) ::: ::: ## Booleans: questions with yes/no answers

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 3 == 3 3 == 4 school == "Princeton" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE [1] FALSE [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} And the answers are a type of their own: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "logical" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.blocktext} `==` asks "are these equal?" `=` is an assignment operator, like `<-` ::: ::: ## Combining booleans: `&`, `|`, `!`

And, or, not: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} TRUE & FALSE TRUE | FALSE !TRUE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE [1] TRUE [1] FALSE ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Comparisons produce booleans, so you can combine questions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (3 > 1) & (school == "Princeton") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Missing values: `NA`

`NA` marks a missing value *inside* your data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- c(4, NA, 5) is.na(survey) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Why not just ask `survey == NA`? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey == NA ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA NA NA ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} "Is this value equal to *unknown*?" — the answer is unknown. Use `is.na()`. ::: ## Even `NA` has a type

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(NA) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "logical" ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} `NA` takes the type of the vector it sits in: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(c(1.5, NA)) class(c("a", NA)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} There's an `NA` for every type (`NA_real_`, `NA_character_`, ...) ::: ::: {.fragment} Usually you don't need to be explicit. ::: ## `NA` is contagious

One `NA` poisons every calculation it touches ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(survey) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Tell summary functions to drop missings first: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(survey, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.5 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.blocktext} You will type `na.rm = TRUE` a thousand times and one day you will be grateful. ::: ::: ## Nothing at all: `NULL`

`NULL` is the absence of an object — not a missing value ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} is.null(NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} `NA` is *something*; `NULL` is nothing at all: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} length(NA) length(NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 [1] 0 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} `NA` holds a place; `NULL` disappears: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(1, NA, 2) c(1, NULL, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 NA 2 [1] 1 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Dates are a type too

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} day1 <- as.Date("2026-08-29") class(day1) ## use YYYY-MM-DD where possible ## but see `format = ` arg of as.Date ## Documentation: ?as.Date ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Date" ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Date math: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} day1 + 7 ## also a date! ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "2026-09-05" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} While *subtracting* two dates is something else: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.Date("2026-12-25") - day1 ## difftime class ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Time difference of 118 days ``` ::: ::: ::: # Vectors ## There are (almost) no scalars for data values

`c()` combines values into a vector ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(5, 10, 15) x length(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 10 15 [1] 3 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Surprise: you've been using vectors all along ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} length(school) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} `school` is a character vector of length 1. ::: ## One type per vector

A vector holds exactly one type. Mix them and R will silently "downcast" where possible. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(1, "two", TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "1" "two" "TRUE" ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} To convert on purpose, cast the whole vector at once: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.character(c(1, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "1" "2" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Most functions are *vectorized*: they work element-by-element without being told explicitly ::: ## Combining text: `paste()`

The *right* way to do `school + "University"`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} paste("R", "Bootcamp") paste0(school, " University") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "R Bootcamp" [1] "Princeton University" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} `paste()` glues with a space; `paste0()` glues with nothing :::
::: {.fragment} It casts numbers to text and vectorizes, all at once: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} paste("Day", c(1, 2, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Day 1" "Day 2" "Day 3" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} And `collapse` glues the *results* into one single string: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} paste("Day", c(1, 2, 3), collapse = ", ") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Day 1, Day 2, Day 3" ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Math is vectorized too

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x * 2 x + x x^2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 20 30 [1] 10 20 30 [1] 25 100 225 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} (`**` also works for powers, but write `^`) :::
::: {.fragment} Comparisons are vectorized — one question, one answer *per element*: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x > 8 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Making sequences

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 1:5 5:1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 4 5 [1] 5 4 3 2 1 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} For more control, `seq()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} seq(1, 9, by = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 3 5 7 9 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Summarizing booleans: `any()` and `all()`

Collapse a vector of yes/no answers into one answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x > 8 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} any(x > 8) all(x > 8) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} "Did *anyone* answer yes?" / "Did *everyone* answer yes?" ::: ::: {.fragment} `TRUE` counts as 1 and `FALSE` as 0 — so you can *count* and *share*: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sum(x > 8) mean(x > 8) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 [1] 0.6666667 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Useful vector questions

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} regions <- c("South", "West", "South", "Northeast") length(regions) unique(regions) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 [1] "South" "West" "Northeast" ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Is a value in the vector? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} "West" %in% regions "Midwest" %in% regions ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} !("Midwest" %in% regions) == ("Midwest" %notin% regions) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Elements in vectors can have names

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grades <- c(math = 90, r_bootcamp = 95) grades ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` math r_bootcamp 90 95 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} names(grades) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "math" "r_bootcamp" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Names are also a way to pull values out: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grades["r_bootcamp"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r_bootcamp 95 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Subsetting by position

`[` pulls out pieces of a vector ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(5, 10, 15, 20) x[2] x[c(1, 3)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 [1] 5 15 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Negative positions *drop* instead: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x[-1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 15 20 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Subsetting by condition

A boolean vector inside `[` keeps the `TRUE` positions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x[x > 8] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 15 20 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} `which()` turns a condition into positions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} which(x > 8) x[which(x > 8)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 3 4 [1] 10 15 20 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Read `x[x > 8]` aloud: "`x`, where `x` is greater than 8" ::: ## Sorting and peeking

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(15, 5, 20, 10) sort(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 10 15 20 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} `head()` and `tail()` peek at the ends. Combine for smallest and biggest: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(sort(x), 2) tail(sort(x), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 10 [1] 15 20 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} `order()` yields the _order_ of a (hypothetical) sort: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} order(x) x[order(x)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 4 1 3 [1] 5 10 15 20 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Matrices ## A matrix is a vector with dimensions

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- matrix(1:8, nrow = 4) m ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] 1 5 [2,] 2 6 [3,] 3 7 [4,] 4 8 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dim(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 2 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} `t()` flips rows and columns: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [1,] 1 2 3 4 [2,] 5 6 7 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Filling by row: `byrow`

`matrix()` fills down the columns unless you say otherwise: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} matrix(1:8, nrow = 4, byrow = FALSE) ## (the default) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] 1 5 [2,] 2 6 [3,] 3 7 [4,] 4 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} matrix(1:8, nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] 1 2 [2,] 3 4 [3,] 5 6 [4,] 7 8 ``` ::: ::: ## Growing a matrix: `cbind()`

Bind on a new column: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cbind(m, 9:12) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 1 5 9 [2,] 2 6 10 [3,] 3 7 11 [4,] 4 8 12 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} A single value gets recycled: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cbind(m, 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 1 5 0 [2,] 2 6 0 [3,] 3 7 0 [4,] 4 8 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## When the lengths don't match

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cbind(m, 1:3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning in cbind(m, 1:3): number of rows of result is not a multiple of vector length (arg 2) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 1 5 1 [2,] 2 6 2 [3,] 3 7 3 [4,] 4 8 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Why the warning? ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.blocktext} Recycling is convenient for single values and dangerous for everything else. ::: ::: ## Matrix math

Arithmetic is element-by-element, like vectors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m * 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] 2 10 [2,] 4 12 [3,] 6 14 [4,] 8 16 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Sums along each dimension: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rowSums(m) colSums(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 8 10 12 [1] 10 26 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Matrix multiplication: `%*%`

Build an N × 1 *column* — now shapes matter: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} v <- matrix(c(10, 20), ncol = 1) v ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [1,] 10 [2,] 20 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} `%*%` matches *inner* dimensions and returns a new shape — (4 × 2) `%*%` (2 × 1) → (4 × 1): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m %*% v ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [1,] 110 [2,] 140 [3,] 170 [4,] 200 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `*` is not `%*%`

Element-wise `*` is different. It wants *identical* shapes, just like `+` or `-` or `/`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m * v ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `m * v`: ! non-conformable arrays ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} (`m * 2` worked because a lone number recycles; a mis-shaped matrix does not) ::: ::: {.fragment} If you mean linear algebra, write `%*%`. ::: ## Subsetting a matrix: `[row, column]`

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m[1, ] m[, 2] m[3, 2] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 5 [1] 5 6 7 8 [1] 7 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Conditions work here too — and count *down the columns*: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m[m > 5] which(m > 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 7 8 [1] 6 7 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Lists ## Lists hold anything

Different types, different lengths, even other lists ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- list() x[[1]] <- 1:5 x[[2]] <- seq(1, 9, by = 2) x[[3]] <- "lists are flexible" x[[4]] <- list(a = "hello", b = "world") ``` :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` List of 4 $ : int [1:5] 1 2 3 4 5 $ : num [1:5] 1 3 5 7 9 $ : chr "lists are flexible" $ :List of 2 ..$ a: chr "hello" ..$ b: chr "world" ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `[[` versus `[`

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x[[3]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "lists are flexible" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x[3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [[1]] [1] "lists are flexible" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} `[[` returns the element itself; `[` returns a smaller *list* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(x[[3]]) class(x[3]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" [1] "list" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Why care about lists? ::: # Data frames ## A data frame is a fancy list

`mtcars` is a data frame built into R — let's borrow it ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df <- mtcars class(df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "data.frame" ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Under the hood: a list of columns, all the same length ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} is.list(df) dim(df) # c(nrow(df), ncol(df)) length(df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE [1] 32 11 [1] 11 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Looking at a data frame

Typing `df` prints all rows. Use `head()` instead: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(df, 3) ## head(df) default is 6 rows ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mpg cyl disp hp drat wt qsec vs am gear carb Mazda RX4 21.0 6 160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46 0 1 4 4 Mazda RX4 Wag 21.0 6 160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02 0 1 4 4 Datsun 710 22.8 4 108 93 3.85 2.320 18.61 1 1 4 1 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} `head()` shows just the first rows (six, unless you say otherwise) — the fastest sanity check there is ::: ## The whole structure: `str()`

One line per column: type first, values after ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str(df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'data.frame': 32 obs. of 11 variables: $ mpg : num 21 21 22.8 21.4 18.7 ... $ cyl : num 6 6 4 6 8 ... $ disp: num 160 160 108 258 360 ... $ hp : num 110 110 93 110 175 ... $ drat: num 3.9 3.9 3.85 3.08 3.15 ... $ wt : num 2.62 2.88 ... $ qsec: num 16.5 17 ... $ vs : num 0 0 1 1 0 ... $ am : num 1 1 1 0 0 ... $ gear: num 4 4 4 3 3 ... $ carb: num 4 4 1 1 2 ... ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} This is usually the first thing to run on any new data (alternatively, `View(df)` in RStudio) ::: ## row and column names in a data.frame

::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} names(df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "mpg" "cyl" "disp" "hp" "drat" "wt" "qsec" "vs" "am" "gear" [11] "carb" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rownames(df)[1:4] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Mazda RX4" "Mazda RX4 Wag" "Datsun 710" "Hornet 4 Drive" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} The car names aren't a column. They live in the *row names* ::: ::: {.fragment} Don't do this. ::: ## Names are yours to change

Assign *into* the attribute: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df2 <- df colnames(df2)[1] <- "miles_per_gallon" names(df2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "miles_per_gallon" "cyl" "disp" [4] "hp" "drat" "wt" [7] "qsec" "vs" "am" [10] "gear" "carb" ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Same trick works for `rownames()` — these are just character vectors you can overwrite ::: ## Grabbing a column: `$`

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df$cyl ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 6 4 6 8 6 8 4 4 6 6 8 8 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 4 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 8 6 8 4 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} `table()` counts values — the fastest first look at a column: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} table(df$cyl) # add a useNA = 'ifany' if you suspect NAs! ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4 6 8 11 7 14 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Two columns give a cross-tab: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} table(df$cyl, df$gear) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 3 4 5 4 1 8 2 6 2 4 1 8 12 0 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `as.matrix()`: what do we lose?

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cars_matrix <- as.matrix(df) cars_matrix[1:3, 1:4] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mpg cyl disp hp Mazda RX4 21.0 6 160 110 Mazda RX4 Wag 21.0 6 160 110 Datsun 710 22.8 4 108 93 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} The row names survive the trip because matricies allow row (and column) names. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(cars_matrix) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "matrix" "array" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Matricies require type for *everything*: a single character column would have turned the whole matrix into text ::: ## Subsetting rows

Data frames take `[row, column]` just like matrices ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df[1:2, c("mpg", "cyl")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mpg cyl Mazda RX4 21 6 Mazda RX4 Wag 21 6 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Conditions filter rows: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df[df$hp > 200, c("mpg", "cyl", "hp")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mpg cyl hp Duster 360 14.3 8 245 Cadillac Fleetwood 10.4 8 205 Lincoln Continental 10.4 8 215 Chrysler Imperial 14.7 8 230 Camaro Z28 13.3 8 245 Ford Pantera L 15.8 8 264 Maserati Bora 15.0 8 335 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Extracting columns, four ways

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(df["cyl"], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` cyl Mazda RX4 6 Mazda RX4 Wag 6 Datsun 710 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} `df["cyl"]` is still a data frame — list subsetting with `[` :::
::: {.fragment} `[[` or `$` or `[, "cyl"]` or `[, 2]`) gives the vector itself: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df[["cyl"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 6 4 6 8 6 8 4 4 6 6 8 8 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 4 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 8 6 8 4 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} And single elements by position: `df[1, 1]` is `` 21 `` ::: ## Build one from scratch

`data.frame()` works like `list()`: name the columns, give equal-length vectors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} schools <- data.frame( school = c("Princeton", "Rutgers"), students = c(5590, 36000) ) schools ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` school students 1 Princeton 5590 2 Rutgers 36000 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Add rows or columns with `rbind()` / `cbind()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} yale <- data.frame(school = "Yale", students = 6645) rbind(schools, yale) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` school students 1 Princeton 5590 2 Rutgers 36000 3 Yale 6645 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Reading and writing data ## Your computer is a tree of folders

Every file lives in a folder, and every folder lives inside another — one big tree (folder = "directory"). ```text /Users/you/ ├── Desktop/ ├── Downloads/ └── Documents/ └── bootcamp/ ├── day-1.R └── data/ └── county_population.csv ``` ::: {.fragment} A file's *path* is its full address — the folders you pass through, joined by `/`: `/Users/you/Documents/bootcamp/data/county_population.csv` ::: ::: {.fragment} (Windows spells it `C:\Users\you\...` but in R, always write `/`; it works on every system) ::: ## Growing up is hard

::: {.fragment} ::: {.blocktext} If you have everything in `~/Downloads`.... ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ![](../assets/its_time.png){fig-align="center" height="420"} ::: ## Where is R standing? The working directory

R always works *from* one folder in that tree — its working directory: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} getwd() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "/Users/ericmm/Documents/GitHub/r-bootcamp/notes" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} A *relative* path gives directions from there. No absolute file path required. ```r county <- read.csv("data/county_population.csv") ``` ("go into `data/`, grab the file" — and `..` means "up one folder") :::
::: {.fragment} Can't find your file? Ask what R can actually see from where it stands: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} list.files() list.files("data") ``` ::: ::: ## Making paths painless

::: {.fragment} ::: {.blocktext} `setwd()` exists — but hard-coded paths break on every other computer. Always assume you're in the project root and make all paths relative. ::: :::
::: {.fragment} * If you have a bunch of scripts, but them in `scripts/` * Then paths to data will be `../data/county_population.csv` * Need a file's full path? *Drag the file* from Finder / File Explorer into the console and the path types itself. ::: ## Our data: county populations

2020 Census population for every US county. Download it [here](https://princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp/data.html) and save it in `data/` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} readLines("data/county_population.csv", n = 3) ``` ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "fips,region,division,pop" [2] "01001,South,East South Central,58805" [3] "01003,South,East South Central,231767" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} A `.csv` is just text: one row per line, commas between values, names in the first line ::: ## Reading it in: `read.csv()`

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} county <- read.csv("county_population.csv") head(county, 3) ``` ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fips region division pop 1 1001 South East South Central 58805 2 1003 South East South Central 231767 3 1005 South East South Central 25223 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Compare with the raw file: `"01001"` became the *number* `1001` — the leading zeros are gone! ::: ## Reading it in, *with arguments*

Tell `read.csv()` what the column really is: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} county <- read.csv( "county_population.csv", colClasses = c(fips = "character") ) str(county) ``` ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'data.frame': 3143 obs. of 4 variables: $ fips : chr "01001" "01003" ... $ region : chr "South" "South" ... $ division: chr "East South Central" "East South Central" ... $ pop : int 58805 231767 25223 22293 59134 ... ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} This distinction is often important if you are joining data, if '0xx' is different from 'xx' etc. ::: ## Watch for coded missingness

Surveys love codes like `-9` or `-999` for "no answer" ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ages <- c(34, -9, 27) mean(ages) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 17.33333 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} `NA` is always better. (Why?) :::
::: {.fragment} `na.strings` translates the codes to `NA` when reading: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- read.csv("survey.csv", na.strings = c("-9", "-999")) ``` ::: ::: ## Other `read.csv()` arguments to know

| Argument | When you need it | |:---|:---| | `header = FALSE` | the file has no column-name row | | `skip = 3` | junk lines (titles, notes) sit above the data | | `nrows = 100` | peek at the first chunk of a huge file | | `fill = TRUE` | ragged files — some rows end early | | `na.strings` | which codes mean "missing" |
::: {.fragment} Every one of these is a question about *your file*. You can use `readLines(path, n = a_small_number)` to inspect the file. ::: ## First look at new data: `summary()`

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(county) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fips region division pop Length :3143 Length :3143 Length :3143 Min. : 64 N.unique :3143 N.unique : 4 N.unique : 9 1st Qu.: 10832 N.blank : 0 N.blank : 0 N.blank : 0 Median : 25698 Min.nchar: 5 Min.nchar: 4 Min.nchar: 7 Mean : 105456 Max.nchar: 5 Max.nchar: 9 Max.nchar: 18 3rd Qu.: 67946 Max. :10014009 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Every column at once: quartiles for numbers, profiles for text. Both `str()` and `summary()` are useful. ::: ## Beyond csv

::: {.small} | Format | Functions | Trade-off | |:---|:---|:---| | `.csv` | `read.csv()` / `write.csv()` | opens anywhere; loses types (ask fips!) | | `.rds` | `readRDS()` / `saveRDS()` | one R object, restored *exactly*; R-only | | `.rda` | `load()` / `save()` | many objects at once; R-only | | `.dta`, `.xlsx` | `haven`, `readxl` packages | Stata and Excel files | :::
::: {.fragment} Careful with `.rda`: `load()` will overwrite existing objects if they have the same name. :::
::: {.fragment} Rule of thumb: share `.csv` with humans, save `.rds` and `.rda` for yourself (and collaborators). :::
::: {.fragment} Sometimes. ::: ## Writing files

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write.csv(county, "county_population.csv", row.names = FALSE) ``` ::: ::: {.fragment} `row.names = FALSE` or you'll get a useless, unnamed column :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} saveRDS(county, "county_population.rds") ## holds one object (compressed) county <- readRDS("county_population.rds") ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} save(county, ..., file = "stuff.rda") ## holds one object (compressed) load('stuff.rda') ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Reasons to prefer one or the other? ::: # R as a calculator ## Summarizing a column

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(county$pop) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 105456.3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} median(county$pop) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 25698 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Functions compose, evaluated inside-out: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(mean(county$pop)) ## alternatively, mean(county$pop) |> round() ... ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 105456 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} And a second argument picks the digits: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(3.14159, 2) ## see also: ceiling, floor, trunc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.14 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Making new columns

Assign into a column that doesn't exist yet — and now it does: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} county$pop_millions <- round(county$pop / 1e6, 2) head(county, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fips region division pop pop_millions 1 01001 South East South Central 58805 0.06 2 01003 South East South Central 231767 0.23 3 01005 South East South Central 25223 0.03 ``` ::: ::: ## The rest of the toolbox

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sd(county$pop) ## see also: var() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 335760.4 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} `log()` and `exp()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} log(county$pop[1]) exp(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10.98198 [1] 2.718282 ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Careful: `log()` is the *natural* log — base 10 is `log10()` :::
::: {.fragment} Every function documents itself: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ?median ``` ::: ::: ## Asking real questions

What share of counties hold a million-plus people? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(county$pop > 1e6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.0155902 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} `mean()` on booleans again — about 1.6% (`sum()` would count them) :::
::: {.fragment} Which county is the biggest? `which.max()` finds the position: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} county[which.max(county$pop), ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fips region division pop pop_millions 1946 06037 West Pacific 10014009 10.01 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Sorting the whole data frame

Give me all the information about the three largest counties: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(county[order(-county$pop), ], 3) ## for readability: # ord = order(-county$pop) # county[ord,] |> head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fips region division pop pop_millions 1946 06037 West Pacific 10014009 10.01 1546 17031 Midwest East North Central 5275541 5.28 1453 48201 South West South Central 4731145 4.73 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `summary()` and beyond

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(county$pop) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 64 10832 25698 105456 67946 10014009 ``` ::: :::
::: {.fragment} Build your own with a named vector: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c( n = length(county$pop), mean = mean(county$pop), sd = sd(county$pop) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n mean sd 3143.0 105456.3 335760.4 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} This gets repetitive if we write the same code for each column -- or for a bunch of different data frames... ::: # Wrap-up ## Monday

Morning: * writing your own functions * loops * `lapply()` and friends * Exercise: putting it all together in base R
::: {.fragment} Afternoon: * Writing professional documents (typesetting with Quarto) * `tidyverse` for working more effectively with data * Exercise: applications of `tidyverse` :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
